I am eternally grateful to Dr. Deepa Katyal and her incredible staff for helping my Koko recover so miraculously and their selfless commitment to the cause of animal pain management. featured_reviews.response_from_owner_text:
We are sorry for your loss. However, this review does not reflect the severity of Coco’s documented condition at presentation. Coco was brought to us only once; subsequent treatment and monitoring were carried out elsewhere, outside our supervision. He was presented after reportedly not eating for 29 days, with vomiting, lethargy, severe kidney values, very high phosphorus, and severe metabolic acidosis.

We had explained the seriousness of Coco’s condition, including a guarded prognosis and suspected AoCKD / IRIS AKI Grade V. The treatment plan, monitoring instructions, recommended investigations with the referring veterinarian, need for repeat checks, follow-up advice, and possible complications were clearly communicated. A provisional ultrasound findings and treatment plan were provided during the consultation itself, so treatment was not held back due to the detailed report.

Coco was subsequently managed elsewhere and, as we understand, euthanized by the primary veterinarian within a few days. Given the severity and instability of Coco’s condition, close monitoring and timely reassessment were essential and were clearly advised. No follow-up updates were shared with us, and further treatment continued elsewhere, outside our supervision. Therefore, it is unfair and incorrect to hold our clinic responsible for an outcome in a patient who was presented in an advanced condition, seen by us only once, and then managed elsewhere. We understand the grief of losing a pet, but repeated reviews under different names for the same case are misleading and unacceptable.

featured_reviews.name: Minal Mankar
featured_reviews.review_text:
About 3 months ago, our 3-month-old puppy Mylo swallowed a large mutton bone from the trash. An initial X-ray at another hospital showed it was stuck in his throat near the neck. He was vomiting and not eating anything, and as time passed, he started breathing strangely, almost as if he was choking. We were extremely worried.

Through a common friend, we connected with Dr. Gaurav at Suyash Pet Clinic, Chembur. Even before we visited, he stayed in constant touch over the phone and guided us calmly. At the clinic, he immediately attended to Mylo, started him on saline, and did another X-ray. He clearly explained the situation, the size of the bone, the endoscopy procedure, and all associated risks, while also reassuring us throughout.

What truly stood out was his patience, kindness, and genuine care—not just for Mylo, but for us as anxious pet parents. He did everything he could to avoid surgery, and thankfully, the endoscopy was successful. Mylo recovered well, and we couldn’t be more grateful.

We had visited another hospital before this and felt very unsure due to their lack of clarity and significantly higher costs. In such emergencies, having a doctor who is both skilled and empathetic is truly a blessing.

Highly recommend Suyash Pet Clinic and Dr. Gaurav without hesitation. Writing this review after 2+ months, with a happy and healthy Mylo ❤️

featured_reviews.name: NIKITA AMAR JHA
featured_reviews.review_text:
My friend and I lost our baby cat due to mycoplasma felis, thanks to her ignorance or apathy that lead to her giving us incorrect and apathetic advice. Our cat, TinTin was a stray and we did the first mistake of taking him to get vaccinated at Dr Prachi’s and the first red flag we noticed in her clinic was her offering dog food to the cat who could barely chew at it. A doctor who charges extravagantly cannot buy two separate bags of dog and cat food? This might seem like a little thing but it is not, because it demonstrates her inconsideration and carelessness, which was soon to resurface in a v serious form. Further our cat which was clearly emaciated was declared to be of healthy weight by her that day. Had she alerted us about his frailness (which is her literal job as a doctor), we could have done something. Our cat came back, and we noticed his reducing appetite day by day. So when my friend took the cat to her right after he skipped a meal, she ran some tests said the situation is critical but at the same time prescribed oral medications and liver sensitive food to him and said vaguely that he will get better in a week and fully better in three weeks. That day was one of the worst days in our baby’s life. He pooped continuously to the point when even blood came out and he suffered from severe diarrhoea. When Dr Prachi was informed of this in a state of panic, she prescribed an antibiotic and asked us to take him to Vetic if there is an emergency. The fact of the matter is that it was an emergency at that time but since she did not take the situation seriously, she made us put our guards down. The next morning, our baby was slowly breathing in the morning and was limp, we rushed to Vetic and met Dr Teja (who is a gem of a person; tried to save Tinu but couldn’t). He put him on IV medication and told us how ORAL MEDICATIONS HAD RUINED his condition and we should never given oral medications in this condition. He suffered from gastritis and internal bleeding. After successive days of continuous IV medication, he even started to get better and started becoming responsive. But since a lot of damage was already done to the baby’s body by the poor diagnosis and treatment done by Dr Prachi, his lungs collapsed on the morning of 30th March. Tinu passed away.
If this doctor is not an expert, she could have let us know earlier. And we would have taken our cat to another doctor. But she didn’t do that. Her carelessness costed our baby his life. Would ask her to introspect the consequences of her actions.

featured_reviews.name: Nimisha C.
featured_reviews.review_text: Lost my cat as she did not give full and proper diagnosis. My cat was suffering from Mycoplasma infection as told by a better hospital I went to after her treatment made my pet suffer even more. The treatment she suggested was oral antibiotics which made my cat's liver condition worse, caused gastritis, internal bleeding and induced extreme diarrhea which he did not have before visiting her (8-9 times in a day, once with blood also). Panicking to see my cat in this condition, I called her at 11:30 in the night, even then she didn't convey the urgency or ask us to take him for IV immediately, but prescribed oral Metrogyl and asked to wait, and go for IV only if diarrhea doesn't stop. This, when she could have told then itself how critical his condition was. Seeing his worsening condition, we rushed him to Vetic, Andheri early next morning, and the doctor there clearly told us that oral medications should not have been given! Dr. Prachi knew his condition was not good because the blood test and kidney and liver function tests came out really poor, and she herself told us that liver was 80% damaged. Despite this, she gave oral medicines, and not through IV. She told us he will start getting better in a week and recover between 3-6 weeks! She didn't even try to diagnose the infection which led to symptoms of jaundice. This is medical negligence and incompetence. If you are incapable of treating a pet, at least be honest and say that, so that we can take our loved pets elsewhere and not lose precious time!!!! You made Tintin's suffering worse instead of reducing it, and your negligence resulted in a situation which could not be reversed easily!! I am writing this review as I don't want anyone to go through this. No precious lives should be lost or suffering induced on precious creatures who can't even speak for themselves, due to a professional's negligence and lack of transparency and incompetency.

Animals have rights too—and it is our responsibility to know and uphold them.
Animal welfare laws are designed to protect animals from cruelty, neglect, and abuse, ensuring they live with dignity and care. When we are informed about these laws, we become stronger voices for those who cannot speak for themselves.

Know a few important animal welfare rules in India:
• Causing cruelty, injury, or abandonment of animals is a punishable offence under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960.
• Feeding or caring for community animals is legal and protected.
• Injured or sick animals must be given timely medical care.
• Animals have the right to food, water, shelter, and freedom from pain and fear.

Being aware is the first step towards action. Let’s stand together as responsible citizens and create a safer, more compassionate society for all living beings.

Worst experience.💔

I rescued a severely injured stray cat who was left to die on the road. One of his legs was badly damaged, and with genuine intention to save his life, I brought him here hoping he would receive proper treatment.

Instead of focusing on immediate care or suggesting alternate support options, I was asked to pay ₹5,000–₹6,000 upfront, while being told the total treatment could cost around ₹22,000. As someone who tried to help purely on humanitarian grounds, this was extremely discouraging.

I clearly explained my financial situation and honestly said that I could manage only ₹600–₹700 from my side, which was my genuine capacity. Unfortunately, there was no flexibility, no discussion about raising donations through their network, social media, or other sponsors — which I believe NGOs usually do.

If NGOs start asking large amounts from people who rescue and bring injured strays, then many good-hearted people will stop helping animals altogether. This defeats the very purpose of animal welfare.

With a heavy heart, I had no option but to leave the cat there, feeling helpless and guilty, knowing he might continue to suffer.

This experience was emotionally distressing and disappointing.

featured_reviews.name: Vishva Shah
featured_reviews.review_text:
We trusted this clinic with our 2-year-old cat during the most critical time of his life, and today we are left with heartbreak, trauma, and serious doubts about the care he received.

Our cat was already battling pleural effusion/FIP-related illness, but after the second drainage procedure done at this clinic, his condition worsened dramatically. Unlike the first drainage done elsewhere after which he breathed better and stabilized this time he developed pneumothorax and his breathing never improved afterward.

We were never properly prepared for how unstable his condition had become post-procedure. We also specifically informed the staff that our cat became extremely frightened and aggressive when touched without us present, and requested that he not be unnecessarily handled while we briefly stepped out. Despite that, he was taken out and handled. When we returned, we were met with his lifeless body.

Maybe no one can say with certainty what would have changed the outcome. But as pet parents who watched the drastic difference between the first and second procedures, we cannot ignore the feeling that mistakes, inadequate handling, or complications during treatment may have contributed to his final deterioration.

Losing a pet is devastating enough. Being left with unanswered questions and guilt afterward makes it even harder.

I hope this clinic learns to communicate more transparently, handle critical patients more carefully, and show greater sensitivity toward animals who are already terrified and struggling to survive.
